analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $20 over three years and phases out lower wages for tipped and disabled workers.
analysis.headline: A bill to raise the federal minimum wage to $20 an hour over three years, with no cosponsors, has sat in committee since the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage in steps from $7.25 to $10, then $13, then $16.50, then $20 an hour over three years. After that, the wage would rise automatically each year by whichever is larger: inflation or GDP growth. It would also gradually eliminate the lower minimum wage for tipped workers, the youth subminimum wage for newly hired workers under 20, and the special subminimum wage that some employers may pay workers with disabilities. The bill was introduced by one senator, sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law, and has received no action since.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly the lowest-paid workers in the country. Anyone earning under $20 an hour would see their pay rise in steps, with the largest gains going to workers earning near today's $7.25 federal minimum, including tipped workers, newly hired teenagers, and workers with disabilities paid under special certificates. Once the wage reaches $20, annual increases tied to inflation or economic growth would keep it from losing value over time.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in scheduled steps to $10, $13, $16.50, and finally $20 an hour over three years, ending a $7.25 federal floor that has not risen since 2009.
Indexes the minimum wage after year three to the greater of inflation or GDP growth, so the wage rises automatically each year without further congressional action.

Gradually raises the base cash wage for tipped workers to $20 and then repeals the separate tipped minimum wage entirely, one day after the final tipped wage step takes effect, and guarantees workers the right to keep their tips.

Raises the minimum wage that may be paid to workers with disabilities under special certificates in steps until it equals the full minimum wage, and sunsets the subminimum certificate program altogether, while barring any new employers from entering it.
Phases out the subminimum wage for newly hired workers under 20, which is currently $4.25 an hour, and repeals that exception once the phase-in is complete.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay low wages would bear the cost of the increases, concentrated among restaurants and food service, retail, and other businesses that rely on minimum-wage and tipped labor, including employers holding special certificates to pay workers with disabilities less. Some of that cost would likely be passed to customers through higher prices, and some businesses might reduce hours or staffing. Defenders of the disability subminimum program argue that some workers now paid under it could lose paid work as certificates expire.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: The increases would fall fastest on small businesses and labor-intensive industries like restaurants, which could respond with higher prices, reduced hours, automation, or slower hiring; the effect is largest in low-cost states where the $7.25 federal wage still binds.

The disability provisions end the subminimum certificate program entirely after six years, and critics of ending it have long argued that some workers in sheltered employment might lose jobs rather than move to competitive employment, even though the bill includes transition assistance and a ban on new certificates.

Indexing the wage to GDP growth as well as inflation could push wages up faster than living costs in strong economic years, an open-ended commitment that employers cannot plan around through the political process.

Tipped workers at high-end restaurants who already earn well above the minimum through tips could see tip-pooling dynamics change, and the six-year phase-in for tipped workers means several years of gradual relief rather than an immediate increase.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is large and direct: tens of millions of workers earning less than $20 an hour would get raises, and the tipped, youth, and disability subminimum wages would eventually disappear. The costs are real but are exactly the tradeoffs every minimum wage increase involves: higher prices, tighter margins, and possible job or hours reductions, with the strongest uncertainty around the phase-out of the disability subminimum. The bill's design is straightforward and includes transition help, but a three-year path to $20 is a much larger increase than Congress has ever enacted, and the bill has attracted no cosponsors from either party, which limits its near-term prospects regardless of its merits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced and has had no cosponsors and no further action since.

narrative.text: Sen. Ruben Gallego introduced the bill in the Senate on February 4, 2026.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No senator has cosponsored the bill, and its only action to date is the committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet; the bill is simply awaiting committee action that has not been scheduled, and the status quo wage floor remains in place for now.

for.name: Sen. Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred on the day of introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no other senator has signed on, so there is no record of party positions; the bill has zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: Restaurants are the largest employer of tipped and minimum-wage workers, and the bill would phase out the tipped subminimum and raise the base wage to $20, directly increasing their labor costs. Customers would likely see higher menu prices as some of that cost is passed through.

industries.industry: Retail, fast food, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: Employers whose payrolls are built around the $7.25 federal floor would face steep, scheduled increases to $20 over three years. Many would raise prices, cut hours, or automate to absorb the cost.

industries.industry: Employers holding disability subminimum certificates (sheltered workshops)
industries.note: The bill ends new certificates immediately and sunsets the program after six years, requiring these employers to pay the full minimum wage. This industry's ability to pay below-minimum wages exists only because of the exemption the bill removes.

industries.industry: Workers with disabilities currently in subminimum employment
industries.note: Their legally permitted wage floor would rise in steps from $5 to the full minimum wage over six years, with transition assistance offered, though the strongest objection is that some could lose sheltered jobs rather than move to competitive employment.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action more than a week after introduction, the bill is very unlikely to move. Minimum wage legislation in this Congress would realistically need broad bipartisan support to overcome Senate procedural hurdles, and none has materialized. The most likely path is that the bill sits in committee for the remainder of the session unless the sponsor builds cosponsor support, which has not happened.
